title: Tax Avoidance by Multinationals
subtitle: How Big Tech pays so little tax
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: The digital giants often pay tiny amounts of tax compared with their profits. It is not always illegal. It is the result of gaps in international law.

hero.hook: In 2014, Apple paid an effective tax rate of about 0.005% in Ireland. How is that possible?

blocks.text: The five giants known as Big Tech, Google, Apple, Facebook (Meta), Amazon and Microsoft, are among the richest companies in the world. Yet, measured against their profits, they often pay far less tax than an ordinary small business.

This is not fraud in the strict sense. It is **tax optimization**, the clever use of the gaps in international law. The mechanism costs states hundreds of billions of dollars every year. Here is how it works, and how the world is trying to answer it.

sections.title: A tax built for factories, not for the internet

blocks.text: The international tax system was designed in the early 20th century for an industrial economy. A company had to own factories or offices in a country, what the law calls a [[permanent establishment]], before it could be taxed there.

Digital business broke that link with territory. A company can now dominate a market, capture the data of millions of users and make enormous sums in a country without owning a single building there. It can then separate the place where it earns its money from the place where it declares it.
In 2014, the American tax authorities found that Microsoft had shifted $39 billion of profit to Puerto Rico through intellectual property rights, saving more than $6.5 billion in tax.

sections.title: Hundreds of billions in lost revenue

blocks.text: According to the OECD, these practices cost public budgets around the world between $100 billion and $240 billion a year, or 4 to 10% of all the corporate tax collected on the planet.

blocks.caption: The European headquarters of the digital giants are often set up in the countries with the lowest taxes

blocks.text: That shortfall forces states to choose between raising taxes on households and small businesses, or cutting public spending on health and education. A local company pays a much higher average tax rate than a multinational, which makes for unfair competition.

sections.title: The response: a global minimum tax

blocks.text: In 2021, under the wing of the OECD and the G20, a historic agreement created a [[15% global minimum tax]]. It targets companies with revenue above 750 million euros: if they pay only 5% in one country, their home country can now claim the missing 10%.

Some countries, France among them, have also created a national tax aimed directly at the revenue of the digital giants. In parallel, multinationals must now publish, country by country, where their employees, their profits and their taxes are. That transparency makes the most glaring mismatches easy to spot.

sections.title: Ireland, Europe's capital of tax optimization

blocks.text: With an official tax rate of 12.5% and secret deals known as [[tax rulings]], Ireland became the European hub of tax optimization. Through a complex structure, Apple paid an effective tax rate of about 0.005% in 2014.

The European Commission ordered Ireland to collect 13 billion euros of unpaid tax from Apple, but the country long refused to take the money, fearing that strict rules would drive corporate headquarters to other parts of the world. Campaigners for tax justice also point out that the 15% rate is still lower than the average in developed countries, and that the poorest countries, often the hardest hit by tax avoidance, will recover only a tiny share of it.

Big Tech long exploited the gaps in international law to pay tiny amounts of tax, costing public budgets up to $240 billion a year. Since 2021 a global minimum tax of 15% has tried to correct the imbalance, but the fight for fairer taxation goes on.
